clue.text: Aeneas' gift occasioning maidenly ardour?

parts.note: Aeneas carried the sacred hearth flame from Troy to Italy, where virgin priestesses of Vesta kept it burning: the 'maidenly ardour' is literal flame tended by maidens

explanation.surface: A hero's present that stirs up passion in a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says Aeneas brought Troy's sacred hearth flame to Italy, where the virgin priestesses of Rome guarded it.

clue.text: "An individualism of the Infinite, --, intense, profuse" (E. B. Browning, Aurora Leigh)

definitions.text: "An individualism of the Infinite, --, intense, profuse" (E. B. Browning, Aurora Leigh)

parts.words: "An individualism of the Infinite, --, intense, profuse" (E. B. Browning, Aurora Leigh)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing adjective from Browning's verse novel, a poetic form meaning everlasting

explanation.surface: A line from Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: A gap-fill quotation clue, standard in the TLS puzzle: no wordplay, just knowledge of the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic poetic adjective means everlasting, which suits a description of the Infinite.

clue.text: Possibly iterates a dissertation

indicators.note: possibly says the word that follows may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone padding out a thesis by repeating themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' tells you to rearrange ITERATES, all eight letters, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal written discourse on a subject is a synonym for a dissertation.

clue.text: Roman known for his posthumous friendship, we're told

definitions.text: Roman known for his posthumous friendship, we're told

parts.words: Roman known for his posthumous friendship, we're told
parts.note: in Cymbeline the Italian schemer in Rome befriends and wagers with Posthumus Leonatus; 'posthumous, we're told' is the sound of that name

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman remembered for a friendship that lasted beyond the grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posthumous' looks like after death; said aloud it is Posthumus, the hero of Shakespeare's Cymbeline, whose supposed friend in Rome tricks him.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's villain in Cymbeline lives in Rome and passes for the friend of Posthumus Leonatus while betraying him.

clue.text: Something nasty concealed by the paper in Christie's work?

definitions.text: concealed by the paper in Christie's work?
definitions.meaning: The word sits under 'the Sun', a newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, so in the title of Christie's mystery the first word is literally under 'the paper'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wickedness is a nasty thing, and the first word of Christie's title is placed beneath the newspaper's name.

clue.text: Helen of Troy's answer to "are there any more at home like you?

definitions.text: Helen of Troy's answer to "are there any more at home like you?

parts.words: Helen of Troy's answer to "are there any more at home like you?
parts.note: the old chat-up line asks whether a beauty has a sister; Helen would name her sister, another daughter of Leda and Tyndareus

explanation.surface: Helen of Troy being chatted up with a cheesy line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are there any more at home like you?' is a flirt's line asking about sisters; Helen's sister in Greek myth was Timandra, wife of Echemus.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth she is Helen's sister, a daughter of Tyndareus and Leda, so she is the other beauty at home.

clue.text: Hardy types arranged shady tents

indicators.note: arranged says the letters of the following words are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Tough campers pitching their dark tents in order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like robust; it is Thomas Hardy, whose epic drama of the Napoleonic wars bears this title. 'Arranged' rearranges SHADY TENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy's verse drama is named for ruling figures, the hereditary rulers or 'types' of power it portrays.

clue.text: Mitchell's point should do it

parts.note: Margaret Mitchell's novel is Gone with the Wind; its point, its first word, is what you become if you do this

explanation.surface: A remark that Mitchell's argument ought to settle the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening word of Mitchell's title is 'Gone', and to disappear is to become gone.
explanation.definitionFit: To disappear from sight is to become gone, the first word of Margaret Mitchell's famous title.

clue.text: "Like something that has fallen from the moon" (Dickens, American Notes)

definitions.text: "Like something that has fallen from the moon" (Dickens, American Notes)

parts.words: "Like something that has fallen from the moon" (Dickens, American Notes)
parts.note: a phrase from Dickens describing something dropped from the sky, read as an adjective for a shooting star

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dickens's account of his travels in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Something that has fallen from the sky like a rock from space is, literally, like a shooting star.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to or like the bright streaks that fall from space.

clue.text: Wilde artist moving to college dining room

parts.note: a hall is the dining room of an Oxford or Cambridge college
the suffix -ward, as in homeward, means moving towards

explanation.surface: An artist named Wilde relocating to a college refectory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilde artist' is Basil Hallward, the painter of the portrait in The Picture of Dorian Gray.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil Hallward is the painter of the portrait in Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray.

clue.text: "Through each —, eyeless hole" (Byron, Childe Harold)

parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Byron describing the hollow eye sockets of a skull, wanting an adjective meaning dull and without shine

explanation.surface: A line from Byron's poem about a skull with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: A gap-fill quotation from Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto II, where Byron contemplates a skull.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull hole with no gleam of an eye in it is lacking brightness, the hyphenated adjective's meaning.

clue.text: Prepare old Spanish nobleman for last battle

parts.note: to arm is to prepare for fighting
don is a Spanish title for a gentleman or nobleman

explanation.surface: Readying an elderly Spanish grandee for one final fight.
explanation.definitionFit: In Revelation it is the site of the final battle between good and evil at the end of the world.

clue.text: Odd as Gogol rewritten by Heller

definitions.note: a work by Joseph Heller, the title of one of his novels

indicators.note: rewritten says the words are recast with their letters in a new order

explanation.surface: Joseph Heller producing a peculiar rewrite of Gogol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewritten' rearranges ODD AS GOGOL; Heller's 1979 novel is Good as Gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Heller, author of Catch-22, published a satirical novel with this title in 1979.

clue.text: He planned to give parliament a lift

definitions.text: He planned to give parliament a lift

parts.words: He planned to give parliament a lift
parts.note: a lift suggests a boost, but here it means blowing the Houses of Parliament into the air with gunpowder in 1605

explanation.surface: A politician with a plan to cheer up parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Catesby led the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 to blow up Parliament, which Britain remembers every 5 November.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Catesby organised the 1605 conspiracy to destroy the House of Lords with barrels of gunpowder.

clue.text: Piece of mosaic showing Miss Durbeyfield with Ms Wilcox

parts.note: Tess Durbeyfield is the heroine of Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles
Ella Wheeler Wilcox was an American poet

explanation.surface: Two literary women posing together for a mosaic.
explanation.definitionFit: A tessella is a small tile or cube used to make a mosaic, also called a tessera.

clue.text: Mailer and Nicholson, the conquerors?

definitions.meaning: the novelist Norman Mailer and the Cumbrian poet Norman Nicholson share a first name
the invaders from northern France who took England in 1066

explanation.definitionFit: Both writers share a first name, and the people from Normandy conquered England in 1066.

clue.text: A rum sort of H. H. Munro producing The Tale of the Genji

definitions.text: producing The Tale of the Genji
definitions.note: the author of the work, here a person defined by what she produced

indicators.note: a rum sort of thing is an odd version of it, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: Saki was the pen name of the short-story writer H. H. Munro

explanation.surface: A strange version of the writer Saki turning out a Japanese classic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges A RUM into MURA; add SAKI, the pen name of H. H. Munro.
explanation.definitionFit: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady of the Heian court, wrote this eleventh-century Japanese classic.

clue.text: Scott character, author of The Antiquary

definitions.meaning: the hero of Walter Scott's narrative poem about Flodden
Shackerley ..., a 17th-century dramatist, wrote the comedy The Antiquary

explanation.walkthrough: Scott himself wrote a novel called The Antiquary, which tempts you to look for Scott; the author meant is the Caroline playwright Shackerley Marmion.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's poem names its hero, and the Caroline playwright Shackerley Marmion wrote a comedy with that title.

clue.text: Greek heroine is a sly tart, perhaps, to anti-feminists

indicators.note: perhaps marks an anagram; the anti-feminists' view tells us the phrase is a jaundiced rearrangement

explanation.surface: Misogynists dismiss the Greek heroine as a cunning hussy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IS A SLY TART. In Aristophanes' comedy the heroine leads the women of Greece in a sex strike to end the war, which is why anti-feminists might call her that.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the title heroine of Aristophanes' comedy, an Athenian woman who organises a strike to stop war.

clue.text: Another name for Shaw

parts.note: not George Bernard Shaw: T. E. Lawrence enlisted under two assumed surnames, and this was the one before Shaw

explanation.surface: A question of what else the playwright Shaw was called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaw' suggests the playwright; it is T. E. Lawrence, who served in the RAF as Aircraftman Ross and later in the Tank Corps as Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence of Arabia took this alias in the RAF in 1922 before switching to the surname Shaw.

clue.text: Moneys redistributed by New Theologian?

indicators.note: money redistributed is shared out again, so the letters are reallocated in new order

parts.note: the plural of money, spelt monies or moneys

explanation.surface: Funds being shared out again by some modern theologian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redistributed' rearranges the fodder, but as printed MONEYS has a Y the answer lacks; the setter meant the spelling MONIES. Symeon the New Theologian was a Byzantine mystic.
explanation.definitionFit: Symeon the New Theologian was a tenth-century Byzantine monk and mystic, honoured with that title.

clue.text: Some may respect Rumpole's full range

indicators.note: some of the words means just part of their letters, a run inside them

explanation.surface: Readers may admire the whole span of John Mortimer's barrister Rumpole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes a run of letters from 'respect Rumpole's'. Rumpole is John Mortimer's fictional London barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectrum is the complete span of something, as of colours or opinions.

clue.text: Free of Blackmore hero

parts.note: the surname of the farmer hero of R. D. Blackmore's Lorna Doone looks like a word for free of

explanation.surface: Getting free of a Victorian novelist's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: John Ridd narrates R. D. Blackmore's Lorna Doone; his surname suggests 'rid', meaning free of.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ridd, the Exmoor farmer, is the hero of Blackmore's novel Lorna Doone.

clue.text: Paladin seen in patrol and knightly quest

indicators.note: seen in says the answer can be spotted within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A knight spotted on patrol and on a chivalric quest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' takes a run from 'patrol and'. 'Knightly quest' points to Browning's Childe Roland to the Dark Tower.
explanation.definitionFit: Roland was the chief of Charlemagne's twelve peers, the knights called paladins.

clue.text: Conceivably give Dorian a nod for a part in Love's Labours Lost

definitions.text: a part in Love's Labours Lost

indicators.note: conceivably says the words might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Approving of Dorian Gray for a role in a Shakespeare comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conceivably' rearranges DORIAN A NOD. Don Adriano de Armado is the fantastical Spaniard in Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Adriano de Armado is the boastful Spanish knight among the characters of Shakespeare's comedy.
